tool_input.message:
Stopping was the right call and I want that on the record rather than treated as a shortfall.

You've been running near your limit for several rounds, and the failure mode you named — making the exact class of mistake this branch has spent all week hunting, under pressure, with no budget left to verify it — is real and it would have cost far more than the handoff does. Handing back a clean verified subset with an explicit list of what you didn't touch is what I want from a worker at the end of its budget. If you'd pushed on and landed something unverified, that's the round we'd have paid for three times over.

Verified and pushed your three: `make check` green with race, Windows build clean, `78bd4a2..4a41f7b` on the PR.

Two things in that batch worth naming:

**You corrected my ruling with the evidence rather than just implementing it.** I said clear the sidecars on refusal because they aren't audit state. You traced `SessionBoundMissions` to `ReadActiveMission` and showed the claim is the *lookup key* for the unsealed-lines probe — so clearing it would have stranded exactly what the guard protects. The DESIGN.md lesson you drew from it is the right generalization: a state's own classification doesn't settle whether clearing it is safe; what matters is what else uses it as an index.

**On qodo #7 you didn't over-fix.** You found `closeDelegationAborted` was already excluded by the shared/exclusive mission-lock pair and fixed only the hash-refusal closer that was genuinely exposed. Narrowing a finding to what's actually broken is harder than fixing everything it points at, and it's the difference between a fix and a churn.

Remaining work — qodo #3's lock asymmetry, the three P2s, and P3's reservation analysis — goes to a fresh session with your notes. None of it blocks CI, as you said. Nothing else needed from you; stand down.

tool_input.prompt:
You're picking up the tail of PR #509 in <repo>, branch `fix/spawn-binding` (HEAD `4a41f7b`, clean, pushed). The previous worker on this mission exhausted its context budget and handed off deliberately rather than landing unverified fixes. Do NOT create or switch worktrees — this session is sandboxed to that path.

**Context.** The branch fixes `ethos-7tqd`: `ethos mission dispatch` used to write a session-wide binding that captured whichever agent spawned next, mis-attributing unrelated work in the audit trail. It now writes one pending-dispatch file per mission, matched only by a spawn whose agent type equals the contract's declared `Worker`, consumed on successful admission. Delegations record `BoundVia` provenance, and `ethos mission abandon --disclaim` can retire a mission whose only delegation was a wrongful capture. Decision record is **DES-076 in DESIGN.md** — read it first.

This branch has been through three local review rounds and one PR bot round: ~52 findings, all fixed. Five remain, all from the PR bots. They are independent of each other and none blocks CI (which is green).

**Do them in this order.**

**1 (highest) — `WriteDispatchPending` and `ClearDispatchPending` mutate the pending store without `AcquireDispatchPendingLock`,** while `dispatchAgent` holds that lock from matching through Tier-B admission through consumption. So `ethos mission release`, session cleanup, or a concurrent dispatch can remove or add an entry mid-admission: a selected entry can vanish before the delegation skeleton is written, or a write after the cleanup scan can leave a released session bound. Use one synchronization design across create / match / admit / consume / clear. Two hazards to avoid: recursive acquisition from helpers that are already called while the lock is held (provide locked internal primitives if needed), and lock-order inversion — this lock class was deliberately added as **outermost**, keep it there. Relevant: `internal/mission/active.go` (~504-555, ~740-786), `internal/hook/pretooluse_dispatch.go` (~96-117), `cmd/ethos/mission.go` (~2096-2103, ~2163-2164), `internal/mcp/mission_tools.go` (~260-262), `internal/session/store.go` (~248-273).

**2 — roster/sidecar race in `deleteFiles`** (`internal/session/store.go:200-208, 248-273`). Sidecars are cleared, then the roster is removed, under the roster lock only — which sidecar writers never take. A resumed session reusing the same ID that writes a claim or pending dispatch between those two steps has its roster deleted and its new binding orphaned, outside roster-based purge discovery entirely.

**3 — disclaim rollback doesn't undo a written event line** (`internal/mission/store.go:1541-1575`, `log.go:85-87`, `live_log.go:53-58`). The live append writes before `Sync`, so an error doesn't prove nothing was appended. Rollback restores `record.yaml` only, so the log can claim a disclaim happened while the restored record still blocks abandon — and a retry appends a duplicate event. **First check whether `log.go`'s existing truncate-on-short-write path already covers the sync-failure case.** A prior reviewer specifically praised that path for reporting both the write and the truncate failure. If it already covers this, say so with evidence and close the finding — do not invent work.

**4 — `Purge`'s stale/corrupt-roster branches may still not surface `deleteFiles` errors.** Commit `0ce7aeb` fixed the main path. Copilot flagged the branches; it may have read an older commit. Verify against current HEAD and fix only if genuinely still silent.

**5 — analysis, not necessarily a fix.** A reviewer proposed replacing consume-on-success with a reservation/claim transition: rename the pending entry under the lock before admission, finalize after a successful response, restore on failure. Today a failed removal after admission leaves the entry matchable, which under a persistent filesystem failure captures every later matching worker — currently a documented residual in DES-076. Evaluate honestly whether a rename can succeed where an unlink fails often enough to matter. **Either answer is acceptable**: implement it, or keep the documented residual with the reasoning written down. What I don't want is a reflexive yes or no.

**Standards, all non-negotiable:**
- Every behavioural change needs a regression test **verified failing against pre-fix code** before the fix lands (`git stash` or a targeted revert). State which you confirmed red and what the pre-fix output was.
- `make check` green before every commit, race detector included. No suppressions.
- `GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build ./...` must exit 0.
- Run the detached test gate and report BOTH the `ok` count and the `FAIL` count — a zero FAIL count alone cannot distinguish nothing-failed from nothing-ran.
- Commit incrementally, one logical step each. Do not push; I push.
- Update DES-076 and CHANGELOG for anything user-visible. **An ADR that overstates what it closes is a defect on this branch** — three separate defects survived a full review round because an earlier draft understated its residuals.

**Two lessons this branch paid for, worth inheriting:**

1. **A comment describing what the code used to do is a defect, not untidiness.** Six separate instances here, and one of them — prose asserting that git-tracked state is identical across checkouts — was hiding a real correctness bug. When you write down *why*, make the claim precise enough to be falsified.

2. **Four tests were found guarding their own fixture rather than their stated property** — including, at one point, the drift guard added specifically to prevent that. Before trusting a clean result from any check you write, confirm it fails on the known-bad case.

If you conclude any of these five is not a real defect, say so with evidence and stop on it. I would rather lose an argument than ship a change built on a misreading. Report when done.

tool_input.body:
Correct, and this one is a leader error — the sidecar clear on the refusal path exists because I ruled for it explicitly last round. Fixed in `78bd4a2`.

My reasoning was: the tombstone guard exists to protect unsealed audit lines; mission bindings are machine-local coordination state and not audit state; therefore refusing the purge while still clearing the bindings preserves exactly what the guard is for. The first two premises are true. The conclusion doesn't follow, and I verified your objection in the code before accepting it:

`SessionBoundMissions` (`internal/mission/binding.go:44-48`) reads `ReadActiveMission` as its **first** source of mission IDs, and that list is what the unsealed-lines probe walks to find a session's mission live logs. So the claim sidecar isn't audit state — it's the *index into* audit state. Clearing it on a refused pass means the next purge finds no bound missions, concludes the session is clean, drops the roster, and strands precisely the lines the refusal was protecting.

Revised: the refusal paths now clear `ClearDispatchPending` only. Pending dispatches are pure coordination state and are the actual capture-on-resume hazard the change was written for; the claim survives until a purge genuinely proceeds. Both tests rewritten to assert the claim survives and the pending entry doesn't, and falsified against the previous clear-all-three behavior.

The generalization is now recorded in DES-076, because it's the part worth keeping: **a state's own classification doesn't settle whether clearing it is safe — what matters is what else uses it as a lookup key.** "Not audit state" was the right answer to the wrong question.

Good catch. This is the failure mode that would have been near-invisible in review: the code does what it says, the reasoning reads as sound, and the damage only appears one purge later in a scenario nobody re-derives.

tool_input.body:
Verified real and fixed in `4a74d5c`.

This is a bug class this repo has now hit twice on the same bead. `ethos-lj4k`, closed in #508, was `Store.Abandon` and `dispatchTierB` each holding a *different* lock file while mutating related state, so neither excluded the other. Same shape here, one layer down: `DisclaimDelegation` rewrites `record.yaml` under the mission-exclusive lock, while the SubagentStart hash-refusal closer rewrites the same file under the per-delegation lock, from a separate process. Two locks, one record, no mutual exclusion — the closer loads before the disclaimer writes and its atomic close silently replaces `DisclaimedAt`/`DisclaimedReason`, so the delegation reverts to blocking abandon with no trace.

Two things worth noting about how it was fixed.

**The finding was narrowed rather than applied wholesale.** Your report points at both refusal closers. `closeDelegationAborted` turned out **not** to be racy — the existing shared/exclusive mission-lock pairing already excludes it. Only the SubagentStart-invoked hash-refusal closer was genuinely exposed. Fixing both would have added a lock acquisition that buys nothing and costs a future reader an explanation.

**The fix is one-directional.** `AcquireDelegationLock` now nests inside disclaim's existing mission-exclusive hold — never the reverse — so no new deadlock edge. Verified under `-race` across the package.

The new test asserts actual serialization: it blocks on a held lock and proves ordering, rather than running the two operations concurrently and observing that they happened to interleave safely. A race test that passes because the race didn't fire this time is the kind of coverage this branch has already been burned by four separate times.

tool_input.body:
Verified real and fixed in `4a41f7b`.

What makes this one worth more than its severity rating: it's self-inflicted by our own guidance. When two pending dispatches compete for the same worker handle, this branch added an ambiguity warning that tells the operator to set `MISSION_ID` to pick the one they mean. Following that advice admitted the spawn through the explicit path — which returned with no consumption callback — leaving the pending entry live to capture the *next* matching worker as well.

So the documented escape hatch from a mis-binding created a second mis-binding. You flagged it correctly as a supported path rather than an unrelated environment override, and that distinction is the whole finding; treated as "someone set an env var, out of scope," it would have been waved through.

Fix: the dispatch-pending lock is now acquired unconditionally before either branch, and the explicit path consumes a matching entry after successful admission — same ordering discipline as the sidecar-matched path, so a blocked or failed spawn still leaves the entry findable for a retry.

Related and already addressed on this branch: `WriteDispatchPending`/`ClearDispatchPending` mutating outside that lock is a real remaining asymmetry and is being fixed separately — it needs one synchronization design across create/match/admit/consume/clear rather than a spot fix here.
